newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serbs promise to join new presidency.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serbs promise to join new presidency.

text.p: Bosnian Serb hardliners will participate in Bosnia's new multi-ethnic national presidency despite having campaigned on a separatist platform, one of their leaders said on Saturday.
International envoys Richard Holbrooke and Carl Bildt received the assurance from Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic in Banja Luka where she voted.
Momcilo Krajisnik, a senior member of the wartime leadership, is the Bosnian Serb candidate for the Bosnian presidency which will also include a Moslem and a Croat.

Plavsic was at Holbrooke's side when he told reporters: "Plavsic told us that Krajisnik, if he wins, will participate in the collective presidency in Sarajevo ... and this is something we need to hear.
"We have got to see Krajisnik, if he wins, come to Sarajevo. I don't believe anything until it happens but the fact is that this is one of the major next steps."
A boycott of the collective presidency by the Bosnian Serbs, who make no secret of their desire for independence, would seriously dent hopes of building ethnic cooperation.
Krajisnik, an experienced politician, is the strongest of the presidential candidates fielded by Bosnian Serb parties.
He could even be the senior member of the collective presidency if rivals to the main Moslem candidate, outgoing President Alija Izetbegovic, drain away too many of his potential votes.
International peacemakers are keen to start building inter-ethnic national government structures in Bosnia as quickly as possible after the elections.

Even if they participate, the Bosnian Serbs are expected to follow a policy of systematic obstruction in which they can expect cooperation from Bosnian Croat hardliners who dislike having been forced into a federation with the Moslems.
Election organisers forced Plavsic to apologise on television on Friday for the secessionist demands made by the SDS during the election campaign.
Plavsic is standing for the separate office of Bosnian Serb president after U.S. pressure forced war leader Radovan Karadzic to leave public life as an indicted war criminal.
The West is still not certain that he does not continue to wield backstage influence.
Holbrooke said he "asked (Plavsic) specifically whether former President Karadzic was still involved and was assured that this was not the case. I hope that is true."
